item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-21
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 21 August 2026 · Welcome to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on the machine learning papers that matter for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 21 August 2026. Here is what crossed HuggingFace Daily and deserves your attention. · Today we have six papers. Two are about making agents get better at themselves during execution. Two are about squeezing more capability out of a model through post-training, one on small-scale reinforcement learning that teaches a dangerous lesson about evaluation, and one genuinely tiny forecaster that is worth your time. · Thinking in a Low-Resource Language: What SFT Builds, What RL Fixes · First, a paper that should make every engineer paranoid about their evaluation harness: "Thinking in a Low-Resource Language," from Alibaba, OpenAI, and NVIDIA. The setup: take three frontier mixture-of-experts models with three-and-a-half to four billion active parameters, and fine-tune them to reason in Greek. On accuracy, almost nothing happens. And here is the killer line from the authors: the benchmark itself is noise at this scale, because changing only the random seed shifts the score by seven-point-seven points. That is larger than every single data and recipe effect they measured. If you are tuning models by a point or two of accuracy, you are tuning noise. · But that null result is exactly the point, because the real changes live where accuracy cannot see. The base models never think in Greek: zero out of a thousand reasoning traces, even when the question itself is in Greek. They answer correctly while reasoning entirely in English. item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-14
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 14 August 2026 · Welcome to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on the machine learning papers that matter for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 14 August 2026. Here is what crossed HuggingFace Daily and deserves your attention. · Six papers today, and there is a theme you will spot immediately: four of them refuse to touch the model weights. They improve the harness, the memory system, the skill library, or the refusal behaviour around a frozen model. The other two are a warning about how easily AI judges are manipulated, and a disciplined recipe for teaching models to say no. · AutoDesign: Optimizing the Harness That Builds the Artifact · First, "AutoDesign," a framework for meta-harness optimization. The setting: turning multimodal input into a structured output, like generating an academic poster from a paper, is really a long-horizon agentic process. Existing harnesses for this are static — designed once by hand and never improved. AutoDesign adds a meta-harness optimizer that guides a code agent to recursively rewrite its own harness based on rollout feedback, aligned with human design priors. · The numbers are striking. On their PosterBench main track, AutoDesign scores seventy-eight point three, beating Claude Design, the closed-source commercial system, by seven and a half points. Across seven controlled configurations, adding the learned harness lifts the average score from fifty-five to sixty-seven.
